analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval for election rule changes in states with recent voting rights violations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced March 5, 2025 with 220 cosponsors — every one a Democrat — and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a markup, vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill restores and updates the Voting Rights Act's "preclearance" system: states and counties with a record of recent voting rights violations would have to get advance approval from the Justice Department or a federal court in Washington before putting new voting rules in place. It also requires pre-approval for specific changes — like redistricting plans, stricter ID rules, or cutting polling places — in areas with large minority populations, makes it easier to sue over maps that dilute minority voting strength, and requires governments to publicly announce voting changes within 48 hours.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — especially Black, Latino, Asian American, Native American, and other language-minority voters — gain stronger tools to challenge discriminatory district maps and voting rules before they take effect, rather than fighting them election by election. DOJ gains power to demand documents and assign federal observers; all voters gain 48-hour public notice of voting changes and published data on polling places and machines. Ordinary voters have no concentrated lobby of their own; the bill was written and backed entirely by House Democrats.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new, race-neutral formula for preclearance: a state where 15 or more voting rights violations occurred in the past 25 years (or 10, if at least one was committed by the state itself, or 3 in a state that runs its own elections) must get DOJ or D.C. federal court approval for 10 years before changing its voting rules.

Requires pre-approval for specific practices in areas with significant minority populations: redistricting changes, stricter ID or proof-of-citizenship requirements, cutting or moving polling places, reducing voting hours (including Sunday voting), shrinking multilingual materials, and new methods for purging voter rolls.

Restores the ability to win vote-dilution lawsuits by writing into law the factors courts use to judge whether a districting scheme weakens minority voting strength, and allows coalition claims by multiple minority groups acting together.

Requires states and localities to publicly announce any voting change within 48 hours, and to publish precinct-level data on polling places, voting machines, and poll workers before federal elections.

Strengthens enforcement: the Attorney General can demand documents and written answers from election officials before suing, federal observers can be assigned to protect bilingual voting rights, and private citizens — not just the Justice Department — can sue over voting rights violations.

analysis.who_pays: State and local election officials in covered jurisdictions bear the main cost: submitting changes for federal approval, publishing notices and precinct data, and defending practices in court. State legislatures lose the power to change election rules unilaterally. The Justice Department, and so federal taxpayers, fund the enforcement workload, and covered jurisdictions' own staffs handle the compliance paperwork.

drawbacks.text: Coverage turns on violation counts over the previous 25 years, so states are constrained for past conduct, and how the formula is applied each year depends on which administration controls the Justice Department — a power future administrations could use unevenly.

In covered jurisdictions, listed voting changes — including tighter ID rules, polling place moves, and redistricting — cannot take effect until the Justice Department or a D.C. federal court approves them, shifting final authority over election administration from states to the federal government. Opponents call this a return of federal pre-approval that the Supreme Court struck down in 2013; supporters call it the remedy the Court asked Congress to build.

New administrative duties fall on election offices: public notice of changes within 48 hours, and published precinct data on machines, poll workers, and demographics — real work for smaller county and municipal offices.
The bill's bar on making voting rules worse than they were applies retroactively to state actions taken on or after January 1, 2021, exposing decisions already made to new legal standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters, the benefits are significant: a working system to stop discriminatory voting rules before an election, rather than after. The costs are real but bounded — compliance paperwork for election offices and a loss of state control over election changes, concentrated in jurisdictions with recent violation records. The most serious honest objection is not cost but design and durability: the coverage formula keys off historical violation tallies and its application rests in the hands of whichever administration runs the Justice Department. How well it protects voters would depend on that department's willingness to enforce it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee in March 2025, and more than a year into the session it has had no committee vote, no floor action, and no scheduled next step.

narrative.text: Rep. Terri Sewell introduced the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act of 2025 in the House on March 5, 2025, with the Democratic leadership and roughly half the chamber signed on as original cosponsors.
All 220 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has added their name.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and the full action history shows nothing since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
Congress is still in session through early January 2027, so the bill is not dead, but a bill that sits in committee without a markup can simply expire when the session ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet — the bill has simply not moved. If it expires, the beneficiaries of that outcome will be state legislatures and election officials who want to change voting rules without federal pre-approval, and the majority party that controls the House agenda.

against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee where the bill was referred, has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill has had no action since its March 2025 referral.

against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: With a majority in the 119th Congress, has brought no voting-rights bill of this kind to the floor and has no members backing H.R. 14, leaving it no path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship split is total: all 220 cosponsors are Democrats and none are Republicans, and with Republicans holding the House majority and the Judiciary chair, the bill has not advanced past its referral.

industries.industry: State legislatures and state election officials
industries.note: The bill takes away their power to change voting rules unilaterally: covered jurisdictions must get Justice Department or D.C. court approval for major changes, publish every voting change within 48 hours, and report precinct-level data. Their institutional interest in keeping sole control of election rules runs against the voters seeking protection from discriminatory changes.

industries.industry: Local election offices (counties, municipalities, school districts over 10,000)
industries.note: They face new compliance duties — preclearance submissions, 48-hour public notices, and published data on machines, poll workers, and demographics — a real administrative cost, though one that exists to inform the very voters they serve. Smaller jurisdictions are exempt from most reporting.

industries.industry: Political parties that draw district maps
industries.note: Redistricting changes in fast-growing minority areas become preclearance-covered, and the bill makes it easier for plaintiffs to win suits claiming maps dilute minority voting strength — directly threatening partisan map-drawing strategies.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority and chairing the Judiciary Committee, and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in this Congress. The closest precedent is the previous version, which passed the House in 2021 but died in the Senate when a procedural vote to cut off the filibuster failed 50-49. Absent a change in chamber control, the likely path is expiration at the end of the session and reintroduction in the next Congress.
